passages.t: Water on thirsty land, and no other Rock
passages.happening:
‘But now listen, O Jacob My servant, Israel, whom I have chosen’ (verse 1). The LORD who formed them from the womb says, do not be afraid, Jeshurun, his chosen (verse 2).

‘For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and currents on the dry ground. I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants’ (verse 3). They will spring up like willows by flowing streams (verse 4). One will say he belongs to the LORD, another will take the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand that he is the LORD's (verse 5).

The King and Redeemer of Israel says, ‘I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me’ (verse 6). Who is like him? Let him foretell what is to come (verse 7). ‘Do not tremble or fear’ (verse 8). God told them long ago, and they are his witnesses. ‘There is no other Rock; I know not one’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Jeshurun is a rare poetic name for Israel, found elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32 and 33, probably meaning upright one, a name of what God means his people to be.

The promise of the Spirit is pictured as water on dry ground. The result is new growth, and people of other nations gladly taking the LORD's name: writing on the hand likely draws on the practice of marking slaves or soldiers with their master's name. Here it is done willingly, out of love.

The claim of verses 6 to 8 is the heart of these chapters. The LORD is first and last, the only God, and the only Rock. The exiles had seen the gods of Babylon in all their splendor. They are told, there is no other.
passages.later: Moses' last words to the people use the same name: ‘There is none like the God of Jeshurun’ (Deuteronomy 33:26). And the risen Christ says, ‘I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last’ (Revelation 22:13).
passages.asks: In the promised future, people write on their hands that they belong to the LORD. Ask what you would write on your hand. And ask whether there is any other rock you are leaning on.

passages.t: Half a log for the fire, half for a god
passages.happening:
‘All makers of idols are nothing, and the things they treasure are worthless’ (verse 9). The craftsmen are only human (verse 11).

The blacksmith works over the coals with his hammers, grows hungry and tired, and has no water (verse 12). The woodworker measures and marks, shapes the wood with chisels and compass into the figure of a man, to sit in a shrine (verse 13). He cuts down a cedar or an oak, or plants a laurel and the rain makes it grow (verse 14).

Part of it is fuel. He warms himself and bakes bread, ‘he even fashions it into a god and worships it’ (verse 15). He burns half of it and roasts meat on it, eats and is satisfied, and warms himself (verse 16). ‘From the rest he makes a god, his graven image. He bows down to it and worships’ (verse 17), and prays to it to save him.

No one stops to think: half of it went in the fire, and should he bow down to a block of wood (verse 19)? ‘He feeds on ashes. His deluded heart has led him astray’ (verse 20), and he cannot ask whether the thing in his hand is a lie.
passages.hearers:
This is the longest satire on idol-making in the Bible. It follows one log from the forest to the oven and the shrine. The same wood cooks dinner and receives prayers.

The blacksmith who makes a god grows hungry and weak. The god cannot even keep its maker fed. The woodworker gives the god a human shape, because he has no other model.

Ancient worshipers were not stupid. But the logic of idolatry, looked at plainly, collapses. The worshiper cannot see it, because his heart has led him astray. The first hearers, who saw Babylon's gods carried in procession, were given words to see through them.
passages.later: A psalm mocks the same: ‘Their idols are silver and gold, made by the hands of men. They have mouths, but cannot speak’ (Psalm 115:4-5). Jeremiah says idols are ‘Like scarecrows in a cucumber patch’ (Jeremiah 10:5).
passages.asks: The man warms himself with half the log and bows to the other half. Ask what you use for ordinary needs that you have also begun to worship. And ask what lie you may be holding in your right hand without seeing it.

passages.t: Return to the LORD, and Cyrus his shepherd
passages.happening:
‘Remember these things, O Jacob, for you are My servant, O Israel. I have made you, and you are My servant; O Israel, I will never forget you’ (verse 21). ‘I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to Me, for I have redeemed you’ (verse 22).

‘Sing for joy, O heavens, for the LORD has done this’ (verse 23). Shout, depths of the earth; break out in song, mountains and forests.

The LORD, their Redeemer, made all things, stretched out the heavens and spread out the earth by himself (verse 24). He foils the signs of false prophets and makes fools of diviners (verse 25). He confirms his servant's word and says Jerusalem will be inhabited and Judah's towns rebuilt (verse 26). He says to the deep, be dry (verse 27). He says of Cyrus, ‘My shepherd will fulfill all that I desire’, and of Jerusalem, ‘She will be rebuilt’, and of the temple, ‘Let its foundation be laid’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The order matters. Sin blotted out comes first, then the call to return. Forgiveness is not the reward for coming back. It is the reason to come back.

Cyrus II, the Great, united the Medes and Persians in the 550s BC, conquered Lydia in the 540s, and took Babylon in 539. His policy was to let deported peoples go home and restore their temples. The book of Ezra records his decree allowing the Jews to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.

Cyrus is called the LORD's shepherd, a title used for Israel's own kings. A foreign king who did not know the LORD would do what the LORD desired.
passages.later: Ezra records Cyrus's decree: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah’ (Ezra 1:2). Long before, a prophet had named Josiah before his birth (1 Kings 13:2).
passages.hard:
How could a prophet in the eighth century BC name Cyrus, who lived about 150 years later?

This is the sharpest form of the question of the book's authorship, and these notes set out each view. Readers who hold that Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote the whole book say he did so by revelation, and that naming Cyrus is not an embarrassment to the text but its argument: throughout chapters 41 to 48, God proves his deity by announcing events before they happen, and naming Cyrus is the climax of that claim. They note a parallel in 1 Kings 13:2, where Josiah is named long before his birth, and point to Josephus's tradition that Cyrus read these words himself.

Most critical scholars conclude that chapters 40 to 55 were written by a prophet during the exile, when Cyrus was already conquering the region, and that the prophet interpreted his rise as God's doing before Babylon fell in 539 BC. On this view the prophecy is still a true word from God, but it speaks into events already under way. Some mediating readers hold that the book grew within Isaiah's tradition and was shaped into its unity over time. Readers of all these views agree on the chapter's claim: the God of Israel, not the gods of Babylon, stands behind the rise and fall of empires.
passages.asks: God blotted out his people's sins and then called them to return. Ask whether you have been waiting to come back to God until you feel forgiven. And ask whether you can see God at work through people who do not know him, as he worked through Cyrus.
